newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO U.S. IN U.S. CENTS/LB, CIF.
Bull (95 Chemical Lean) 92 -3 on last week
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO JAPAN IN U.S. CENTS/LB CIF.
Chilled grassfed fullsets 127 -4 on last week
AMLC COMMENTARY: Price rises in the cattle saleyards virtually ground to a halt this week, as the value of beef in export markets slid backwards.

In Queensland, quieter demand from processors appeared to be at the centre of the correction in values, although the quality of cattle was not up to the high standard of last week and probably contributed to the price falls. The Queensland cattle market indicator fell two points during the week to 93 points, which is the equivalent of a 2-3c/kg liveweight price fall.
On the export scene, prices were on the back foot again in Japan, as end user demand continues to languish. Chilled grassfed fullset export prices decreased 4 USc/lb to 127 USc/lb.

In Japanese wholesale markets, the recent appreciation of the yen has assisted price falls for imported beef. This will be of some assistance in stimulating end user demand. The depreciation of the yen, which occured during most of this year, has generally eroded the benefits of lower imported beef prices to Japanese consumers.

US slaughter continues to rise and, given the decline in cow slaughter, it is valid to assume tht the increase is due to larger number of steers and heifers. During the past month boxed beef prices have fallen around 3 USc/lb from their April highs, pressuing packer margins. This has led to packers cutting bids for cattle over that time by around 3 USc/lb to 65 USc/lb.

Statistics released by Statistics New Zealand show that the New Zealand beef herd fell by around 6.4 percent in the year to 30 June 1996, to 4.85 million head. This is the first drop in New Zealand cattle numbers since 1989. The dairy herd continued
to rise through, reaching an all-time high of 4.17 million, up 1.8 percent.
